questions.what: When a colleague asks what the product is, can the reader answer in one sentence that tells them what it does?
Reading the gain, can the reader tell what the product would let them do, and so whether it is for them?
When a colleague asks why this product and not another way of doing the same work, can the reader name what it does differently that brings the gain?
Before installing, can the reader tell what the product does not do that they might have expected of it?
After the walkthrough, can the reader tell that the product would give them, on work of their own, the gain the opening promised?
Starting with nothing set up, can the reader install the product by the README's steps alone, and tell that it works?
For each gain and the idea, can the reader see in the figure of how the product works how the product keeps it?
When the reader needs more than the README gives, such as fuller use or a change to the product, can they tell from it where to read next?
Can the reader tell from the README the terms on which they and their team may use the product?
Reading from the top, does the reader find each answer just when they come to need it, so they can stop as soon as they have what they came for?

decisions.what: Who reads the README, and how is each reader spoken to?
decisions.decided: The UX's two users. The person is spoken to as you throughout. The maker AI is spoken to as you in a paragraph of its own that opens with whom it is for, and the README names it a maker AI there. Differs from the old README, which spoke to a plugin, not to an AI.

decisions.what: Which name does the README give each thing, and where does the reader learn it?
decisions.decided: A point: one thing the plan must settle, a fact or a decision, defined in the gain where first used. The design: the plan's goal with every point settled under it, defined in the idea. The design file: the file design-tree.json that holds the design. A maker AI: defined in its paragraph. The AI that makes the work: the AI that later makes the person's work from the design file. Each keeps the one name from start to end, in the figure too. Differs from the old README, which named the file a design tree and called the thing it holds by the same name.
grounds: dev/pin/ux.md:10-12 "A point of a plan is one thing the plan must settle [...] The design is the plan's goal with every point settled under it."

decisions.what: What is Pin, in one sentence?
decisions.decided: Pin is a Claude Code plugin that settles every point of your plan before an AI starts to make it, finding each fact itself and asking you only the decisions that are yours, one at a time. A colleague who hears only this can say: it settles the plan up front, looks up facts itself, and asks me only my own decisions, one by one. Differs from the old summary by naming the facts Pin finds, so the colleague does not take Pin for a list of questions.
grounds: readme.json Q1 step 1: "Write one sentence on its own line under the title, such as \"<Name> is a <kind> that <does what>.\", saying what the product does with no feature names or mechanisms."
readme.json Q1 step 2: "Ask whether a colleague who hears only the sentence could say what the product does."

decisions.what: What does the person gain, and how can a reader tell Pin is not for them?
decisions.decided: For you when you are about to have an AI in Claude Code make something larger than a quick change, such as a feature or a document, and want it to make what you mean. Pin settles every point as you mean it before the work starts; you decide only the points that are yours and confirm each fact Pin finds; the AI that makes the work has nothing left to guess, and you do not explain a point again while it works. A last sentence tells the reader outside the group: for a quick change you would just ask for and check, Pin adds a step you do not need. Differs from the old gain by that last sentence and by "as you mean it".
grounds: dev/pin/ux.md:19-20 "O1: The person has every point of their plan settled as they mean it before any work starts, asked only what is theirs."
plugins/pin/README.md:6 "takes more than one sitting, such as a feature or a document"
readme.json Q2 step 2: "Ask whether a reader outside that group can tell from it that the product is not for them. If not, name the group and the work more closely."

decisions.what: What does the maker AI gain?
decisions.decided: For you if you are an AI that is to make something for a person, such as a skill or a subagent of a plugin, and want its design settled with that person before you build. You hand Pin the work's goal, the questions the work must answer, and what you have settled. Pin keeps what you settled, the goal among it, and does not ask the person it again. You pass each point Pin gives you to the person as given, and the answer back word for word. You get back a design settled with the person, and you build the work on it as given. An AI with no person to ask is outside the group, as each point that is the person's waits for their answer. Differs from the old README, which said only that the plugin gets back a design it can build on.

decisions.what: What does Pin do that another way of doing the same work does not?
decisions.decided: One paragraph names the two other ways: an AI that starts to make the work from the request and asks as questions occur to it, and a plan written up front whose gaps are filled with assumptions; either way a point no one raised is guessed and comes back as rework. Pin instead settles the whole plan from its goal down before any work starts, and its result is the design. Five parts follow, each with what it ensures: from the goal down (the design holds each point the work needs and none that serves nothing); facts found, decisions asked (Pin finds and shows each fact, settles what follows from the goal and the facts, and asks you only a decision where two ways serve as well or one is hard to undo, with a recommendation); one point at a time, in order; the whole design confirmed, each point with who settled it; kept in a file, checked after each answer, so a stopped run goes on and the AI that makes the work reads it. Differs from the old idea, which named only a chat as the other way, had no part for the whole design confirmed, and gave the check script a part of its own.

decisions.what: What might the reader expect of Pin that it does not do?
decisions.decided: Four non-goals, each a thing a reader could expect: Pin does not make the work, and ends once you confirm the design; it does not judge whether a decision is good, its check sees only that the design holds together; it does not decide what is yours, and a point you leave unanswered stays open; it asks no several questions in one message and sets no limit on their number, and told to wrap up it leaves the open points marked open. Kept from the old README.

decisions.what: How does the reader install Pin and tell that it works, and how does a maker AI's plugin get it?
decisions.decided: The marketplace's two commands; claude plugin list then lists pin@ccpm, and in a new session /pin:down is one of the commands. A plugin whose skill or subagent is a maker AI lists Pin in the dependencies of its plugin.json, and installing that plugin installs Pin. Q6 step 3, the install from nothing, is left to whoever may install: this README was made where nothing could be installed.

decisions.what: Which scenario does the walkthrough run, and which point does Pin ask?
decisions.decided: The UX's O1 on the notes app: the person types /pin:down, confirms the goal, confirms one fact found, and decides one point that is theirs, whether the JSON is one array or one object a line, which Pin puts with a recommendation; Pin settles the rest itself, such as keeping text the default, shows the whole design with who settled each point and no ID, and keeps it in the design file. The result shows the gain: every point settled, one asked of you, one settled from a fact you confirmed, one that followed from the goal and was not asked. Differs from the old walkthrough, which asked the person which fields each note has, a point that follows from the text output and so is not theirs, and showed IDs to the person.

decisions.what: What does the figure of How it works show, so each gain and the idea can be seen in it?
decisions.decided: An SVG with Pin as one shaded box, and around it you, a maker AI, your repository, the design file and the AI that makes your work. Lines: you give Pin your plan, then each answer; Pin gives you one point at a time, then the whole design to confirm (one at a time, only yours); Pin finds each fact in your repository (facts found); Pin writes each point with who settled it into the design file, which holds the goal and every point under it (from the goal down, kept in a file); a maker AI gives Pin the goal, its questions and what it settled, and gets each point for you, then the design (O2 gain); the maker AI passes each point to you as given and your answer back word for word; the maker AI and the AI that makes your work build on the design file (settled before the work). Pin's box says it settles itself what follows from the goal and the facts. Differs from the old figure, a flowchart that showed a subagent and check.py inside Pin and no maker AI.

decisions.what: In what order do the parts stand?
decisions.decided: readme.json's order: the summary, the person's gain, the maker AI's gain, the idea and the non-goals under no heading, so a reader can stop before Requirements; then Requirements, Installation, Walkthrough, How it works, Documentation, Development and License. The question each part leaves is answered by the next: is it for me, then how is it different, then what will it not do, then what do I need, then how do I install it, then what do I get, then how is it kept, then where next, then on what terms.
